title: Bashō walks into a ramen shop 200 years too early | Timeslip Ramen Ep. 1
title_b: Rainy night at a cozy pixel ramen shop 🍜 lofi, rain & Japanese history (Ep. 1)
description:
Japan's most famous poet walks in from the year 1689, a kappa wants cucumbers, and you meet the regulars: Haru the cook, Kon the fox, Mika and Gen-san.

Tonight at the counter:
· Matsuo Bashō (1644–1694), haiku poet, on the road to the Deep North
· a kappa, river yōkai with a dish of water on its head

Chapters
0:00 Cold open
0:22 Opening
1:38 Bashō
4:29 Kappa
6:40 Next time

豆知識 · Facts on screen (with sources)
· Kitsune Udon · fox noodles: Fried tofu (aburaage) has long been offered to foxes at Inari shrines, so in folklore foxes love it. Noodles topped with it are called kitsune: fox.
  Source: Wikipedia: Kitsune, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kitsune
· Matsuo Bashō · poet, 1644–1694: In spring 1689 Bashō left Edo (now Tokyo) with his companion Sora. They walked about 2,400 km in some 150 days: the journey of Oku no Hosomichi, The Narrow Road to the Deep North.
  Source: Wikipedia: Oku no Hosomichi, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oku_no_Hosomichi
· Ramen · a newcomer: Ramen grew out of the Chinese noodle soups of Japan's port towns. Rairaiken, usually called the first ramen shop, opened in Asakusa, Tokyo, in 1910, with cooks from Yokohama's Chinatown.
  Source: Tokyo Weekender: Chūka soba and the Chinese roots of ramen, https://www.tokyoweekender.com/art_and_culture/history/chuka-soba-ramen-chinese-history/
  Source: SoraNews24: Japan's first ramen restaurant reopens, https://soranews24.com/2020/08/13/japans-first-ever-ramen-restaurant-which-closed-44-years-ago-is-reopening-this-fall/amp/
· The Old Pond · 1686: Furuike ya / kawazu tobikomu / mizu no oto: "an old pond / a frog jumps in / the sound of water." Bashō wrote it in 1686. It may be the best-known haiku of all.
  Source: Bashō Memorial Museum, Iga: chronology, https://www.basho-bp.jp/en/?p=10
· Kappa · the dish on its head: A kappa keeps water in a dish on top of its head. If the water spills, it loses its strength until the dish is refilled. Kappa are so polite that if you bow, they bow back... and spill it.
  Source: World History Encyclopedia: Kappa, https://www.worldhistory.org/Kappa/
· Kappamaki: Kappa are famous for loving cucumbers. That's the usual reason given for calling a cucumber sushi roll kappamaki, though nobody knows exactly when the name stuck.
  Source: World History Encyclopedia: Kappa, https://www.worldhistory.org/Kappa/
  Source: Sushi-pedia: kappa, https://www.sushi-pedia.com/en/glossary/kappa

Words on screen
· 暖簾 noren: The cloth curtain over a shop door. Out means open; taken in means closed.
· いらっしゃいませ irasshaimase: "Welcome!" Called out to everyone who walks into a shop.
· ただいま tadaima: "I'm home." Said as you walk back in.
· おかえり okaeri: "Welcome back." Said to someone coming home.
· いただきます itadakimasu: Said before eating: "I humbly receive."
· 模試 moshi: A mock exam (short for mogi shiken), graded A to E.
· お邪魔します ojama shimasu: "Sorry to intrude." Said when entering someone else's place.
· 蕎麦 soba: Thin buckwheat noodles, eaten in Japan for centuries.
· 色紙 shikishi: A stiff square board for poems, pictures and autographs.
· いってらっしゃい itterasshai: "Take care!" Said to someone heading out who will come back.
· 冷やし中華 hiyashi chūka: Cold ramen noodles with toppings, usually a summer dish.

Timeslip Ramen is a pixel-art ramen shop on a rainy street corner whose door opens onto any century. Haru keeps the broth hot, Kon the fox keeps trying to look human, Mika studies for her exams and Gen-san refuses to believe any of it.

title: The samurai who was late on purpose | Timeslip Ramen Ep. 2
title_b: Closing time at a cozy pixel ramen shop 🍜 rain, a samurai & a tanuki (Ep. 2)
description:
Miyamoto Musashi turns up five minutes before closing, exactly as planned. Then a tanuki in a very convincing disguise has a score to settle with Kon.

Tonight at the counter:
· Miyamoto Musashi (c. 1584–1645), swordsman and author of The Book of Five Rings
· a tanuki, shapeshifting raccoon dog of folklore

Chapters
0:00 Cold open
0:24 Opening
0:48 Musashi
3:06 Tanuki
5:38 Closing

豆知識 · Facts on screen (with sources)
· Miyamoto Musashi · 1584–1645: In 1612 Musashi fought Sasaki Kojirō on Ganryūjima, a tiny island. The famous telling says he arrived hours late, with a wooden sword he had carved from a boat's oar. Accounts differ on almost everything.
  Source: Britannica: Miyamoto Musashi, https://www.britannica.com/biography/Miyamoto-Musashi-Japanese-soldier-artist
  Source: Discovery UK: Sasaki Kojirō and Ganryū Island, https://www.discoveryuk.com/mysteries/who-was-sasaki-kojiro-and-what-happened-at-ganryu-island/
· The Book Of Five Rings: Late in life Musashi wrote down his strategy in The Book of Five Rings, still read today. He was also a fine ink painter: his shrike perched in a dead tree is one of his best-known works.
  Source: Britannica: Miyamoto Musashi, https://www.britannica.com/biography/Miyamoto-Musashi-Japanese-soldier-artist
· Tanuki · a real animal: The tanuki is the Japanese raccoon dog, a wild member of the dog family. In folklore it's a shapeshifter; in the tale Bunbuku Chagama, a tanuki turns itself into a tea kettle.
  Source: Wikipedia: Tanuki statue, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanuki_statue
· Kitsune · foxes and their tails: In Japanese folklore, the more tails a fox has, the older and wiser it is. Some tales say a fox grows another tail only after living 100 years, and learns to take human form at about that age.
  Source: Wikipedia: Kitsune, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kitsune
· The Lucky Tanuki: Pottery tanuki from the town of Shigaraki stand outside shops and inns all over Japan for luck and prosperity: straw hat against bad weather, a sake flask, a big round belly.
  Source: Wikipedia: Tanuki statue, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanuki_statue

title: Hokusai moved house 93 times. Then he came for ramen | Timeslip Ramen Ep. 3
title_b: Cozy pixel ramen shop on a rainy night 🌊 Hokusai, yōkai & lofi (Ep. 3)
description:
The painter of The Great Wave needs a place to sit (he has moved 93 times). Grandpa's old umbrella turns one hundred and wakes up. And a customer rows in on a soup bowl.

Tonight at the counter:
· Katsushika Hokusai (1760–1849), painter of The Great Wave
· a kasa-obake, an umbrella that turned one hundred
· Issun-bōshi, the one-inch boy of the fairy tale

Chapters
0:00 Cold open
0:16 Opening
0:34 Hokusai
2:25 The umbrella
3:38 Issun-bōshi
5:08 Closing

豆知識 · Facts on screen (with sources)
· Katsushika Hokusai · 1760–1849: Hokusai moved house about 93 times, reportedly because he hated cleaning, and used at least 30 names. In his seventies he called himself Gakyō Rōjin: "the old man mad about painting".
  Source: Sotheby's: 21 facts about Katsushika Hokusai, https://www.sothebys.com/en/articles/21-facts-about-katsushika-hokusai
· The Great Wave: The Great Wave belongs to Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji, a series Hokusai began around 1830, in his seventies. He hoped his best work would come at 110. He died at 88.
  Source: Sotheby's: 21 facts about Katsushika Hokusai, https://www.sothebys.com/en/articles/21-facts-about-katsushika-hokusai
· Tsukumogami · things that come alive: In folklore, an object that reaches its hundredth birthday can gain a soul. The kasa-obake is an old paper umbrella with one big eye, a long tongue and one hairy leg. Mostly it likes to startle people.
  Source: Uncanny Japan: haunted artifacts (tsukumogami), https://uncannyjapan.com/haunted-artifacts-tsukumogami/
· Issun-bōshi · the inch-high samurai: In this old tale a boy one inch tall sets off for the capital in a bowl, paddling with a chopstick, with a needle for a sword. He beats an oni, and its magic mallet makes him full size.
  Source: Wikipedia: Issun-bōshi, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Issun-b%C5%8Dshi

title: Who ate Japan's first ramen? | Timeslip Ramen Ep. 4
title_b: Rainy holiday night at a cozy pixel ramen shop 🍜 Mito Kōmon & lofi (Ep. 4)
description:
Labour Thanksgiving Day. Tokugawa Mitsukuni claims the first bowl of ramen in Japan, Gen-san meets his TV hero, and Hiraga Gennai has a slogan (and a spark) to save a slow Monday.

Tonight at the counter:
· Tokugawa Mitsukuni (1628–1701), lord of Mito, "Mito Kōmon"
· Hiraga Gennai (1728–1780), inventor, writer and slogan-maker

Chapters
0:00 Cold open
0:16 Opening
1:07 Mitsukuni
2:59 Gennai
4:44 Closing

豆知識 · Facts on screen (with sources)
· Labour Thanksgiving Day · 23 November: Japan's day for thanking workers got its modern name in 1948. It grew out of Niiname-sai, an ancient festival of thanks for the harvest.
  Source: Wikipedia: Labor Thanksgiving Day, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labor_Thanksgiving_Day
· Mito Kōmon: On television, Mitsukuni roams Japan in disguise, punishing crooked officials; the series Mito Kōmon ran from 1969 to 2011. The real lord gathered scholars to write a huge history of Japan, the Dai Nihonshi.
  Source: Wikipedia: Tokugawa Mitsukuni, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokugawa_Mitsukuni
· Tokugawa Mitsukuni · 1628–1701: The lord of Mito is often called one of the first people in Japan to eat ramen. Historians are doubtful: noodles were served in Kyoto as early as 1488, and ramen as we know it took shape around 1910.
  Source: Wikipedia: Tokugawa Mitsukuni, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokugawa_Mitsukuni
  Source: Tokyo Weekender: Chūka soba and the Chinese roots of ramen, https://www.tokyoweekender.com/art_and_culture/history/chuka-soba-ramen-chinese-history/
· Hiraga Gennai · about 1729–1780: Legend says an eel shop asked Gennai how to sell eel in summer, and he suggested a sign: today is the Day of the Ox. Japan still eats eel on that day. Whether he really did, nobody knows.
  Source: Hiroko's Kitchen: Hiraga Gennai and the eel, https://hirokoskitchen.com/blogs/all/marketing-genius-hiraga-genna-unagi-eel
  Source: Wikipedia: Hiraga Gennai, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiraga_Gennai
· The Elekiter · 1776: Gennai spent years rebuilding a broken Dutch electrostatic generator and showed it off in 1776: the first in Japan. People came to see the sparks, and it was used as a medical device.
  Source: IEEE Milestone: Elekiteru, first electrostatic generator in Japan, 1776, https://ethw.org/Milestones:Elekiteru:_First_Electrostatic_Generator_in_Japan,_1776

Words on screen
· 模試 moshi: A mock exam (short for mogi shiken), graded A to E.

title: Hachikō came in from the rain | Timeslip Ramen Ep. 5
title_b: A dog, the rain and a warm bowl 🐕 cozy pixel ramen shop (Ep. 5)
description:
A very good dog waits by the door, and Gen-san softens. Then Urashima Tarō has been away "three days" and is carrying a box nobody should open.

Tonight at the counter:
· Hachikō (1923–1935), the dog who waited at Shibuya
· Urashima Tarō, the fisherman of the old tale

Chapters
0:00 Cold open
0:16 Opening
0:34 Hachikō
2:10 Urashima Tarō
3:57 Closing

豆知識 · Facts on screen (with sources)
· Hachikō · 1923–1935: Every evening Hachikō met his owner, Professor Ueno Hidesaburō, at Shibuya Station. Ueno died in May 1925. Hachikō kept coming back to the station, morning and evening, for almost ten years.
  Source: nippon.com: Hachikō, the faithful dog, https://www.nippon.com/en/japan-glances/jg00137/hachiko-the-faithful-dog.html
· The Statue: A bronze statue of Hachikō was put up at Shibuya Station in 1934, while he was still alive. It was melted down during the war and rebuilt about three years after it ended.
  Source: nippon.com: Hachikō, the faithful dog, https://www.nippon.com/en/japan-glances/jg00137/hachiko-the-faithful-dog.html
· Urashima Tarō: A fisherman rescues a turtle and visits the Dragon Palace under the sea. In the version children learn today he stays three days; back home, about 300 years have passed. Older versions say 700.
  Source: Wikipedia: Urashima Tarō, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urashima_Tar%C5%8D
· The Box: The princess gives him a box and warns him never to open it. He opens it, white smoke pours out, and he is suddenly old. An early form of the tale is in the Nihon Shoki, under the year 478.
  Source: Wikipedia: Urashima Tarō, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urashima_Tar%C5%8D

title: The thunder god wants your belly button | Timeslip Ramen Ep. 6
title_b: Thunderstorm at a cozy pixel ramen shop ⛈️ Japanese folklore & lofi (Ep. 6)
description:
Kaguya-hime orders the impossible. Raijin storms in and Gen-san finally stops calling it cosplay. And a little girl by the window has been there all along.

Tonight at the counter:
· Kaguya-hime, the princess from the Moon
· Raijin, god of thunder
· a zashiki-warashi, the child spirit of a lucky house

Chapters
0:00 Cold open
0:16 Opening
0:32 Kaguya-hime
2:06 The storm
3:24 The house spirit
4:16 Closing

豆知識 · Facts on screen (with sources)
· The Tale Of The Bamboo Cutter: Written in the 9th or 10th century, the oldest surviving Japanese monogatari. An old man finds a tiny girl in a shining bamboo stalk. She sets her five suitors impossible tasks, then returns to the Moon.
  Source: Wikipedia: The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tale_of_the_Bamboo_Cutter
· Mount Fuji: Before she leaves, Kaguya-hime sends the Emperor an elixir of immortality. He has it burned on the highest mountain. Legend links the name Fuji to "immortal", and says the smoke still rises.
  Source: Wikipedia: The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tale_of_the_Bamboo_Cutter

豆知識 · Facts on screen (with sources)
· Yuki-onna · the snow woman: A woman all in white who appears on snowy nights. Lafcadio Hearn's book Kwaidan (1904) made her famous abroad; a tale from 1685 already describes skin "so white it seems transparent".
  Source: yokai.jp: Yuki-onna, https://yokai.jp/en/yokai/yuki-onna
  Source: Wikipedia: Kwaidan, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kwaidan:_Stories_and_Studies_of_Strange_Things
· Sugawara No Michizane · 845–903: A great scholar, exiled to Dazaifu in 901. After his death he was honoured as Tenjin and became the god of learning. Students still pray at his shrines before entrance exams.
  Source: Wikipedia: Sugawara no Michizane, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugawara_no_Michizane
  Source: japan-guide: Dazaifu Tenmangū, https://japan-guide.com/e/e4851.html
· The Common Test: Japan's national university entrance exam is held over a weekend every January. For many students, autumn and winter are cram season.
  Source: Wikipedia: Common Test for University Admissions, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_Test_for_University_Admissions
· The Flying Plum: Michizane loved plum trees. Before leaving Kyoto he wrote a poem to his own: when the east wind blows, send me your scent. Legend says the tree flew after him to Dazaifu.
  Source: Wikipedia: Sugawara no Michizane, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugawara_no_Michizane
  Source: japan-guide: Dazaifu Tenmangū, https://japan-guide.com/e/e4851.html

豆知識 · Facts on screen (with sources)
· The 47 Rōnin: In 1703 (31 January by today's calendar) 47 masterless samurai led by Ōishi Kuranosuke avenged their lord. To fool spies, Ōishi had pretended to live a careless life. Japan remembers them every 14 December.
  Source: Wikipedia: Forty-seven rōnin, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forty-seven_r%C5%8Dnin
· Chūshingura: Their story became Chūshingura, retold on stage and screen ever since. They are buried together at Sengaku-ji temple in Tokyo, which holds a festival for them on 14 December.
  Source: Wikipedia: Forty-seven rōnin, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forty-seven_r%C5%8Dnin
· Kitsune · foxes and their tails: In Japanese folklore, the more tails a fox has, the older and wiser it is. Some tales say a fox grows another tail only after living 100 years, and learns to take human form at about that age.
  Source: Wikipedia: Kitsune, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kitsune
· Izumo No Okuni · kabuki begins: In 1603 Okuni and her troupe began dancing a bold new kind of show on the dry riverbed of Kyoto's Kamo River. It became kabuki. In 1629 women were banned from the kabuki stage; it has been all-male since.
  Source: Wikipedia: Kabuki, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kabuki
